meta.title: Who really said "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edison never said it this way. The genuine 1910 remark was “I know several thousand things that won’t work” — the “10,000 ways” line is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work'?
meta.ogDescription: The sentiment is Edison’s, but the wording isn’t. His documented 1910 remark was “I know several thousand things that won’t work.”

answer.label: Not Edison’s words — a later paraphrase of a real remark
answer.sourceLine: The optimistic sentiment is genuinely Edison’s and is documented as early as 1910, but he is not recorded saying this polished sentence. According to Quote Investigator ↗, the earliest and best version of the anecdote — from the 1910 biography Edison: His Life and Inventions, as told by his associate Walter S. Mallory — has Edison saying “I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won’t work.” The rounded-up “10,000 ways that won’t work” wording is a later retelling, filed under “Disputed” by Wikiquote ↗.

source.excerpt: He said: ‘Results! Why, man, I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won’t work.’
trail: The earliest attestation is the 1910 biography Edison: His Life and Inventions by Frank Lewis Dyer and Thomas Commerford Martin, quoting associate Walter S. Mallory, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
The count varies wildly across retellings — 700, 999, 1,000, 10,000 and 50,000 have all appeared — a classic sign of a paraphrase snowballing over time, per QI ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ places the exact “10,000 ways that won’t work” sentence in its Disputed section, citing J. L. Elkhorne, “Edison — The Fabulous Drone,” in 73 Vol. XLVI, No. 3 (March 1967).
source.excerptNote: The 1910 version, recounted by Edison’s associate Walter S. Mallory in Edison: His Life and Inventions, during the multi-year effort to develop a storage battery. This is the source Quote Investigator judges most reliable; note “several thousand,” not “10,000.”

source.rightsNote: The polished sentence “I have not failed. I’ve just found 10,000 ways that won’t work” cannot be tied to a specific documented Edison source; its earliest known appearance is a 1967 magazine retelling, and it reads as an anonymous paraphrase. Because the exact wording’s origin is unknown, we assert no copyright status. (The authentic 1910 remark, by contrast, appears in a public-domain book.)

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: About Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was a prolific American inventor and entrepreneur whose laboratories produced the phonograph, a commercially practical incandescent lamp, and systems of electric power distribution. He held over a thousand US patents and was famous for an iterative, trial-and-error method — the very working style that gave rise to this quote. His remark about failed experiments arose from his years-long effort to perfect a storage battery.

misattribution.heading: What Edison actually said
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication pinned on a famous name — the sentiment is authentically Edison’s. What’s wrong is the exact wording, which is a tidied-up, inflated paraphrase of a real remark.

items.why: No primary source records Edison saying “I have not failed. I’ve just found 10,000 ways that won’t work.” Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed, with an earliest citation only from 1967.
The 1910 account says “several thousand,” and other versions give 700, 999, 1,000 or 50,000. The round “10,000” is one of many escalating variants, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine 1910 remark, recounted by Edison’s associate Walter Mallory, was “I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won’t work” — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Edison spent years running exhaustive trial-and-error experiments — most famously testing thousands of materials for the lamp filament and, later, for a nickel-iron storage battery. The idea that each failed test was a step forward, not a defeat, genuinely captured his method, which is why the paraphrase feels so true to him.

Because the sentiment is authentic, the neatened-up “10,000 ways” version spread through motivational books and speeches until it eclipsed the messier real quotation — a reminder that a quote can be true in spirit and still not be something the person ever actually said.
